# AI Agents at Work: What Holiday Extras and Block Show Us

> **In short:** Holiday Extras says its employees' AI agents, which it calls "dots," produce reports and flag problems before anyone asks. Block says its open source Buzz workspace lets people and AI agents collaborate in the same conversations.

Imagine opening your laptop and finding the report you needed already waiting, along with a note about the email you forgot to answer. Two recent official announcements describe workplaces where this kind of help is becoming normal.

## What an AI agent is

An **AI agent** is an AI program that does more than answer questions. It can look up information, use connected apps and work through a task step by step. Think of it as a capable assistant who reads your to-do list, not just your questions.

## Example 1: A travel company's daily helpers

Holiday Extras, a UK travel technology company, shared how its staff use what it calls "dots." According to the company, one dot noticed a new app feature had launched and pulled performance data on its own. The VP of AI Innovation, Liam Thompson, said he didn't have to ask for it.

The dots work with connected tools. The company describes one dot pulling data from **Google BigQuery** (a service for storing and searching large amounts of data) through a **plugin** (an add-on that links one app to another).

Another employee, David Lee, talks with his dot during his morning commute. He can ask it to run a report, and the company says the results are ready when he reaches his desk. When some **API keys** (secret codes that let one program access another) needed retiring, his dot searched his email and listed the people who might be affected. David didn't have to rebuild that list from old threads.

## Example 2: A shared space for people and agents

Block, the payments company, describes a different approach. Its open source workspace, called Buzz, puts employees and AI agents in the same group chats and one-on-one conversations. Users can create an agent, choose the **model** (the AI brain behind the agent) and bring it into a discussion with colleagues.

Block also says Buzz can use a range of models through one connection, provided by Databricks Unity Gateway. Some are **open-weight models**, meaning their underlying files are publicly available. Block describes one setup where a more capable model coordinates several smaller, cheaper models. The company says it is still experimenting with which combinations work best.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life**: Think about recurring tasks you repeat each week, like gathering notes or summarizing messages. Those are good candidates to hand to an agent later.
- **For your business or work**: Before connecting an agent to email, files or chat, check with your employer about which accounts are allowed. Both companies stress connected company data, so access rules matter.
- **If you're just getting started**: Start with a low-stakes task, such as asking an AI tool to turn your rough meeting notes into a short checklist. Review the result yourself before you rely on it.
- **If you already use it**: Ask your agent to remind you of unanswered messages and to explain where a past answer came from. Keep a short note of what you have shared with it.

## Wrap-up

Holiday Extras and Block both describe AI agents that work with people, not just for them. The lesson for everyday workers is that the most useful agents are connected carefully, checked regularly and given clear, specific tasks. Today, pick one repetitive task you do at work and write down exactly what you would want an assistant to finish for you. That list is your starting point.
